passage.text: Sand dunes are one of the most recognizable parts of certain sandy beaches. Dunes are important because they provide coastal lands with natural protection against wind, waves, and storm damage. Sand dunes also provide places for plants and animals to live. For example, seabirds like to nest in dune grasses. Sand dunes are also beautiful to look at for people who enjoy nature. But what exactly are sand dunes? And where do they come from?

Dunes are actually just piles of sand that are formed when wind and waves move sand onto the beach. First, strong waves pick up the sand and wash it up onto the beach. Once the sand has been dropped on the beach, it is moved and carried by the wind. Over time, wind blows the tiny grains of sand into large piles. A dune is made!

Weather can change the size and shape of coastal dunes, so beaches can change with the seasons. In the winter, bigger storms make stronger waves. These strong winter waves pick up and carry more sand, but they leave less of it on the beach. This causes the beach to get steeper and its dunes to become smaller. However, when summer comes, gentle waves leave more sand on the shore, and the beach takes on a shallower slope. More sand building up on the beach leads to bigger dunes.

Since the wind is usually blowing all day near the shoreline, the shape of the dune is constantly changing. Over time, dunes will grow, shrink, and move depending on the way the wind is blowing. If a strong wind blows grass onto a dune, then the grass may start growing there. The grass's roots and stems then help to trap the sand in the same spot, which makes the dune more stable against the wind.

passage.text: Many people argue that the brain is the most important organ in the body. It controls what we think, what we feel, and what we do all day. For example, your brain is in charge of keeping your balance, helping you talk, and moving the muscles in your body. When you sleep, however, your brain is free from doing most of its daytime tasks. So what exactly does your brain do when you are asleep?

The brain keeps working and thinking all night long. If you have to make an important decision, some people might tell you to "sleep on it." Your brain never shuts down, so it is always busy helping you process information. If you go to bed facing a tough decision, you might wake up and know what you should do. This is because you figured some things out while you were asleep.

Your brain does a lot more than help you make decisions while you are asleep. It also uses that time to help you learn and remember information better. During sleep, the brain goes back over new information that you learned during the day. This information is moved from one area of the brain to another to form a longer-lasting memory. So whenever you learn something new, it can be a good idea to get a good night's rest afterward. It might help you when you need to remember the information later.

When you're asleep, your brain can also clear out toxins that build up during the day. Toxins are dangerous chemicals that can harm your body. For example, toxins in the brain can lead to memory loss. When you sleep, your brain acts kind of like a dishwasher. At night, it fills with a liquid that cleans away these harmful toxins. That way, your brain can do all of its important tasks the next day. With all of the important things that the brain does at night, it's no wonder that humans spend a third of their lives asleep.

passage.text: Many people argue that the brain is the most important organ in the body. It controls what we think, what we feel, and what we do all day. For example, your brain is in charge of keeping your balance, helping you talk, and moving the muscles in your body. When you sleep, however, your brain is free from doing most of its daytime tasks. So what exactly does your brain do when you are asleep?

The brain keeps working and thinking all night long. If you have to make an important decision, some people might tell you to "sleep on it." Your brain never shuts down, so it is always busy helping you process information. If you go to bed facing a tough decision, you might wake up and know what you should do. This is because you figured some things out while you were asleep.

Your brain does a lot more than help you make decisions while you are asleep. It also uses that time to help you learn and remember information better. During sleep, the brain goes back over new information that you learned during the day. This information is moved from one area of the brain to another to form a longer-lasting memory. So whenever you learn something new, it can be a good idea to get a good night's rest afterward. It might help you when you need to remember the information later.

When you're asleep, your brain can also clear out toxins that build up during the day. Toxins are dangerous chemicals that can harm your body. For example, toxins in the brain can lead to memory loss. When you sleep, your brain acts kind of like a dishwasher. At night, it fills with a liquid that cleans away these harmful toxins. That way, your brain can do all of its important tasks the next day. With all of the important things that the brain does at night, it's no wonder that humans spend a third of their lives asleep.

passage.text: Being a wild animal can be really tough. Spending the day or evening searching for food takes a lot of work. Animals also have to stay clear of predators, protect themselves against the weather, and take care of their young. All of these jobs can take a lot of energy. So what do animals do when their food and water is in short supply?

Some animals conserve their energy through a deep sleep called hibernation. During hibernation, an animal's breathing rate and heartbeat slow down to help it save its strength. Its body temperature will also lower for the same reason. In this state, the animal sleeps so deeply that it cannot easily be woken up. Many animals that rely on plants and insects for survival hibernate during the winter. For example, some species of frogs, bats, and snails will hibernate when the weather turns cold and plants and insects die. Some animals only hibernate for a few days, but others can hibernate for months at a time.

Another way for animals to save energy when there is little food is to enter a state of sleep called torpor. Torpor is similar to hibernation, except the sleep is lighter. During torpor, animals can be woken up, but they might be irritable. In fact, some animals get angry enough to attack whatever has awakened them. Many species of bears and birds enter torpor during the winter months. For example, black bears spend weeks before winter eating extra food to prepare for their torpor. This allows them to survive up to one hundred days without eating or drinking.

Not all animals need to conserve energy during the winter. Some animals need to rest up during the summer months, when there can be high heat and droughts. A deep sleep that happens during a hot or dry period is called estivation. Before estivation, an animal looks for a shady, moist, and cool place to sleep. This type of place will help the animal save energy, and most importantly, will provide the water it will need to survive. Earthworms, hedgehogs, crocodiles, and salamanders use estivation to survive hot, dry weather.

These tiny animals are bright and colorful, allowing fish to easily spot them in the water. Cleaner shrimp have a mutualistic relationship with fish, meaning that the shrimp and the fish both get something by working together. The fish get cleaned by the shrimp, and the shrimp get meals from the fish that they clean.

The shrimp remove parasites from the fish. Parasites are tiny sea creatures that attach to fish and cause them harm. The parasites are too small for the fish to remove on their own, but the parasites are the right size to make a perfect meal for a little shrimp. The shrimp uses its tiny claws to pick the dangerous parasites off the fish, and then it eats the parasites.

If a fish has parasites and wants to be cleaned, it looks for a brightly-colored cleaner shrimp waiting on a rock. When the fish swims up to the rock, the cleaner shrimp does a strange dance. The shrimp rocks its body from side to side, and it waves its front legs in the air as if to say, "Fish Cleaning Service! Come right in!" This dance sends a signal to the fish that the shrimp is hungry and willing to clean the parasites off the fish. The fish then changes its color from light to dark. This color change provides a signal to the shrimp that the fish wants to be cleaned.

Cleaner shrimp do a thorough job of cleaning each fish. They will clean a fish from head to tail, and they will even climb into a fish's mouth to clean it. However, large fish could be dangerous for these tiny shrimp, so the shrimp have to be picky about which fish they choose to clean. They will only dance and wave to a fish that does not appear threatening. Also, they will wait until the fish darkens the color of its scales before starting the job. For example, guitar players have to do many things at once while playing music. They use their eyes to read the music, their fingers to pick at the strings, and their ears to listen to the tunes. Different parts of their bodies are working in unison. The more musicians practice, the better their brains get at doing all these things at once. Their brains get stronger and can help the musicians pay attention, solve problems, and remember things more easily.

When you listen to your favorite music, your brain produces a chemical called dopamine that makes you feel good. Listening to music can also be calming. A soft song or melody can help you relax when you are upset. For example, many people sing lullabies to babies. These soft songs can calm babies and help them stop crying.

In addition to making you feel better, music can help relieve pain in your body. Researchers have found that people feel less pain when they are listening to music they enjoy. Researchers have found that the more you like the music you're hearing, the less pain you feel!
